title: Why homemade water filters can be dangerous
h1: Clear water, sand and charcoal: why homemade filters can be dangerous
dek: A bottle of gravel, sand and charcoal makes water look clean. What the CDC, the National Park Service and the EPA say a filter has to do, what a homemade one can't prove, and what to do instead.
description: Why clear water isn't safe water and why homemade sand or charcoal filters can't be relied on, using CDC, National Park Service, EPA and FEMA guidance.
recheck: If CDC, NPS or EPA revise their filter guidance, or at the next quarterly source sweep.

source_use.cdc-water-hiking: Clear water can be unsafe; boiling is best, then filter-and-disinfect; the rated pore sizes and NSF 53/58 certification; viruses are not removed by portable filters; reverse osmosis; UV needs clear water.
source_use.nps-purify-water: Never drink untreated natural water even if it looks clean; filtration alone does not purify; filters are screens; filter cloudy water before boiling; filter care.
source_use.cdc-water-safe: Clearing cloudy water with a cloth, paper towel or coffee filter, or by settling; pore sizes; follow filtering with a disinfectant; fuel, chemicals and radioactive material.
source_use.ready-water: Settle or strain before treating; boiling and chlorination do not remove heavy metals, salts and most chemicals; distillation does.
source_use.epa-emergency-disinfection: Boiling or disinfection will not destroy heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals.
source_use.cdc-find-clean-water: CDC's emergency water page identifies potentially usable household sources including the water-heater tank and melted ice, and warns that fuel- or chemical-contaminated water cannot be made safe through household boiling or filtration. Cited only for those source alternatives and contamination limits.
